It is that NOTHING RECORDED WHICH SECRET A RUNNING RUNNER RESOLVED. runner.json is deliberately secret-free and stays that way - its own header explains why a world-readable file is not where a credential goes - and the consequence nobody had drawn is that a runner whose secret diverges from the data directory's runner.key for any reason becomes permanently unauthenticable with no evidence on disk saying so. runner/session-key.ts is the fix: the runner writes the secret IT ACTUALLY RESOLVED, at the moment it resolved it, under hardenOwnerOnly - the same function, the same proven ACL, the same refusal to start when the ACL cannot be verified. Written BEFORE the endpoint exists, so there is never a moment at which a runner is reachable and nothing on disk says how to stop it, and cleared on graceful shutdown, so a session key on disk means a runner IS alive rather than once was. runner.json also gains channel_secret_fingerprint - SHA-256 truncated to 16 hex, no preimage, pinned by a test - which turns a bare 401, indistinguishable from a wedged runner or a foreign process on the pipe, into a named answer BEFORE a caller connects. Exit 0 clear, exit 3 held. THE VERB SET IS FIXED, which is what ADR 0007's first follow-up said belonged here. It listed six and specified none, saying the set 'belongs with the deploy bridge, where there is something to validate against'; MAR-484 wrote `connect` and left the rest as vocabulary for an implementation that did not exist. lib/deploy/verbs.ts is that implementation: install, start, stop, status, collect, connect, in one closed array beside the arguments each carries and the check BOTH ENDS run. tests/host-record.test.ts's by-value pin on HOST_VERBS FIRED when the set widened from ['connect'], which is that assertion doing its job - a closed set is only worth anything if adding to it is a change somebody has to make in one place and defend. NOTHING VARIABLE REACHES argv, AND THAT IS STRONGER THAN VALIDATING IT. ADR 0007's rule is 'DASH chooses which operation, never what to run'; the mechanism here is narrower and easier to check - a verb's arguments do not go on the command line at all. They travel as one JSON envelope on the child's stdin, so the only strings ssh can be made to interpret are the fixed options sshArgv composes, the destination, and a verb drawn from a closed array. argv is where option injection lives (lib/hosts.ts already refuses a leading - on every component for that reason) and a bundle's file list could never have gone there anyway. `connect` is the ONE exception and it is forced: its stdin IS the HTTP conversation, so a helper that drained stdin first would consume DASH's first request and wait forever for an end that never comes. Its bundle id rides on argv having passed the same check as everything else, over an alphabet that cannot spell a separator, a traversal, a drive letter or a leading -. AN IDENTIFIER IS NOT A PATH. bundle_id and agent_id are opaque tokens; the helper joins them to a root IT chose and never receives a directory. That is MAR-507's rule - the renderer names a kind of file and never a file - pointed at a machine DASH does not administer, where the sharper version applies: a payload that could name a directory is a payload that could name /etc. The file names INSIDE a bundle are the one place a path travels, and they are checked with runner/path-guard.ts's inspectComponent PER SEGMENT. Per-component rather than inspectPathSyntax on the whole string, because that one answers about a path a caller chose and so requires an absolute one - a bundle name is relative by construction and would be refused as not_absolute before any interesting rule ran. Per-component is also the stronger question: .., a colon opening an alternate data stream, a trailing dot Windows silently strips, a control character that truncates a name inside a native call, and every reserved device name at any depth are each properties of one segment. Checked on the HELPER's side rather than only in DASH, and that is the load-bearing word: a rule living only in the sender is a rule the host does not have. THE HELPER IS A BOUNDARY AGAINST DASH ITSELF, not against the host, and the ADR amendment says so rather than inflating it. DASH holds a key that could run anything there. What the closed set rules out is DASH turning a deploy into arbitrary remote execution: `start` runs `node start.mjs` because the HELPER decided that, not because a request said so - runner/README.md's sentence moved one machine over. There is no verb taking a command, no verb taking a path, and no branch passing a caller-supplied string to a shell. Before MAR-520 the only thing on the far end of that would have been a signal - the force-kill AGENTS.md forbids, performed on a machine nobody is watching, against the process holding somebody's agent history. MAR-520 made the runner record the channel secret it actually resolved under an owner-only proven ACL beside its endpoint file, so the helper authenticates to the runner's own POST /shutdown, which is DASH's own Stop button's route one machine over. THE ENROLLMENT STEP: host.probe on a record whose host_fingerprint is null no longer dials. Refusing writes nothing - that is structural, not a code path: nothing happens unless host.trust is called. THE HONESTY IS THE POINT. Trust on first use proves nothing; a fingerprint fetched over the connection it describes is self-consistent by construction. So the copy says 'DASH cannot check this for you - anything answering at this address could say the same thing, so this is the one part only you can confirm.' A screen with a fingerprint and a Confirm button and no such sentence teaches people that clicking yes IS a verification. A test asserts that sentence and that the state is never worded as an error. VERB RESOLUTION IS DECIDED AND RECORDED (acceptance bar 3): FORCED COMMAND, not namespaced verbs. The allowed-keys line is restrict,command="/opt/orchestratedash/dash-host" <key>. Namespacing (dash-status) solves the collision of English words on PATH and nothing else - the key would still be a general shell credential. command= solves it by removing the question (no PATH entries at all) and does what namespacing cannot: ADR 0007's promise that DASH chooses which operation, never what to run, was about DASH's own code being unable to compose a command and said nothing about what the key could do in other hands. sshd runs the helper whatever the client asks, so a key exfiltrated from this machine cannot open a shell there. restrict does the boring half - no port forwarding, agent forwarding, X11, pty or user rc - and is the switch rather than a hand-written list so whatever OpenSSH adds next release is off too.
